articles.body: Rates & Surcharges Top Right Maersk clarifies Trinidad and Tobago port configuration for feeder cargo November 27, 2026 Facebook Twitter WhatsApp Linkedin Email Maersk has outlined the current port configuration in Trinidad and Tobago for cargo transported on its Calypso Feeder and Soca Feeder services. Under the arrangement, shipments will use either Port of Spain or Point Lisas depending on the direction of the cargo and whether it is moving between Trinidad and Tobago, Guyana or Suriname. The applicable port configuration is as follows: Cargo movement Port in Trinidad and Tobago Imports into Trinidad and Tobago Port of Spain Exports from Trinidad and Tobago Point Lisas Exports from Trinidad and Tobago to Guyana Port of Spain Imports from Guyana into Trinidad and Tobago Point Lisas Exports from Trinidad and Tobago to Suriname Port of Spain Imports from Suriname into Trinidad and Tobago Point Lisas Maersk has asked customers to confirm the applicable port when planning cargo deliveries and upcoming shipments on the two feeder services. The Calypso Feeder connects Trinidad and Tobago with ports including Manzanillo and Paramaribo, while the Soca Feeder provides connectivity between Georgetown and Point Lisas. TAGS A.P. articles.body: VLCC Supply Builds as Gulf–China Loadings Hold Steady in International Shipping News 27/11/2026 VLCC earnings fell first on Atlantic routes in Week 45 and then on Gulf routes in Week 46. Over the same period, Signal Ocean’s net-supply data showed more VLCCs available for Arabian Gulf–China loading. Net supply for the Arabian Gulf–China trade averaged 93.2 vessels in 1–22 November, 13.2% above the full-October average of 82.3 and 8.8% above the same period of 2025. Spot and relet vessels, a subset of net supply, rose 23.4% to an average of 61.5. Net supply reached 106 on 11 November, the highest since 20 July, and was 86 on 22 November. Arabian Gulf–China loadings averaged 5.8 cargoes a day in 1–22 November, the same as in 1–22 October and 25% below the same period of 2025. Details are in the Cargo Demand section. Chart 1. VLCC net supply for the Arabian Gulf–China trade and its spot/relet component, daily, 1 August–22 November 2026, with October and 1–22 November averages; Arabian Gulf–China crude cargoes loaded per week, 2026 and the same weeks of 2025.Source: Signal Ocean net supply (VLCC, Arabian Gulf–China) and cargo flows. Weeks run Monday to Sunday. Recent weeks may be revised as more cargoes are recorded. VLCC Earnings Recover from Week 46 Lows VLCC earnings averaged lower in Week 47, with a sharper decline on the US Gulf–China route (TD22), down 13.2% WoW to $246,000/day, compared with a 4.7% decline to $1.07 million/day on Middle East Gulf–China (TD3C). The weekly average TD3C/TD22 earnings ratio widened from 4.03 to 4.37, against a 12-month average of 2.89. Between 13 and 20 November, TD22 earnings increased by 11.4% to $258,000/day, while TD3C rose by 3.1% to $1.09 million/day, narrowing the earnings ratio to 4.21. Compared with 8 October assessments, TD3C and TD22 earnings remained 22.9% and 59.5% lower, respectively. Chart 2. Daily TD3C and TD22 TCE assessments and their ratio, 24 November 2025–20 November 2026. Shading marks 16–20 November. Source: Baltic Exchange TCE assessments via Signal Ocean. Averages of five daily assessments in each week; the ratio row averages daily ratios. Freight: Gulf-Loading Suezmax and Aframax Ease While VLCC earnings increased across all three benchmarks between 13 and 20 November, Suezmax and Aframax earnings on Gulf-loading routes continued to weaken. TD23 fell 5.4% to $619,000/day, and TD8 declined 6.3% to $320,000/day. Since 8 October, earnings across the three East of Suez loading routes have declined by 18–29%, compared with approximately 60% on the two Atlantic VLCC routes. TD3C earnings remain above $1 million/day, compared with less than $300,000/day on both TD22 and TD15. Chart 3. Percentage change in TCE by route: left, 13 to 20 November 2026; right, 8 October to 20 November 2026.Source: Baltic Exchange TCE assessments via Signal Ocean. Route summary: selected crude benchmarks Baltic Exchange TCE assessments via Signal Ocean for the 13 and 20 November closes; USD/day rounded to the nearest $1,000. Changes are calculated from unrounded values. Cargo Demand: Gulf Flat, US Gulf Thin Arabian Gulf–China. 127 cargoes loaded in 1–22 November, against 128 in 1–22 October, or about 5.8 cargoes and 11.1 million barrels a day. Weekly loadings in November ranged from 36 to 43 cargoes. Compared with the same period of 2025, daily cargoes were 25% lower and volumes 22% lower. Arabian Gulf–China loadings were broadly unchanged from the corresponding period of October, while VLCC net supply for the same trade averaged 13% above the full October average. The freight correction therefore coincided with a larger visible vessel pool and broadly stable observed Gulf–China loadings. Crude cargoes loaded: Arabian Gulf–China and US Gulf–China Signal Ocean cargo flows by load date, covering all vessel sizes. Daily averages are calculated using calendar days. November figures are provisional. Recorded loadings exclude forward cargo enquiries and fixing activity. US Gulf–China. Seven cargoes loaded in 1–22 November, against 13 in 1–22 October and 22 in the same period of 2025. One cargo loaded in the week to 22 November. At 0.3 cargoes a day, loadings are below a third of the 2025 rate for the same period. TD22 rose 11.4% in Week 47 without an increase in recorded US Gulf–China loadings. Chart 4. Crude cargoes loaded per day, Arabian Gulf–China and US Gulf–China, by month, 2024–2026; November 2026 covers 1–22 November. Source: Signal Ocean cargo flows by load date; all vessel sizes. Partial-month data are provisional. Westbound Ballasters Increase as VLCC Supply Builds Westbound ballasting activity increased across the VLCC and Suezmax segments in the week to 21 November. Active westbound VLCC ballasters rose from 45 to 53 vessels, with 47 originating from the Far East. Brazil and South Africa accounted for 39 vessels combined, representing nearly three-quarters of the westbound fleet. A more pronounced increase was recorded in the Suezmax segment, where westbound ballasters rose by 67% from 42 to 70 vessels, including 30 heading towards the West African Atlantic Coast and 10 towards South Africa. Despite the increase in westbound ballasting, 83% of VLCCs remained East of Suez, against a typical share of 75%. West-to-East laden movements remained elevated, with 90 VLCC arrivals recorded for November, compared with 57 in September. In the Aframax segment, westbound ballasters remained unchanged at 59 vessels, of which 38 were heading towards the US Gulf. Meanwhile, the US Gulf Aframax tonnage list contracted by approximately 72%, from 46 vessels on 23 October to 13 on 21 November. Chart 5. Active westbound VLCC, Suezmax and Aframax ballasters on 14 and 21 November, and their destinations on 21 November. Ballasters are vessels in transit, not vessels available to load immediately.Source: Signal Ocean, 22 November 2026. “Other destinations” is the segment total minus the listed destinations. Ballaster counts cover westbound vessels and use a different vessel population from the Arabian Gulf–China net-supply data. As of 6 November, VLCC and Suezmax utilisation remained below their corresponding 2025 levels, although both exceeded their Q3 2026 averages. Aframax/LR2 utilisation recorded the largest year-on-year increase among the three segments, reaching 53.9%, against 45.2% a year earlier. Chart 6. Fleet utilisation by segment, 2026, 2025 and the 2023–2025 average, through 6 November 2026.Source: Signal Ocean fleet utilisation; international-trading crude tankers, all age groups. Hormuz Freight Watch: Macro Risks Efforts to reopen the Strait of Hormuz via diplomatic channels remain unresolved as of 24 November. Qatar has restarted its role as mediator after discussions with American and Iranian representatives, yet Tehran continues to insist that negotiations proceed only if Washington fulfills its demands, which feature the removal of the US naval blockade on Iranian ports. Meanwhile, on 18 November, the Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) reaffirmed its severe regional maritime threat assessment, cautioning that additional hostile incidents could occur. Even with active diplomacy resumed, ongoing security risks continue to inflate war-risk insurance premiums, extend voyage turnarounds, and restrict shipowner willingness to take on Gulf cargoes. Consequently, a political resolution on its own may not instantly restore pre-conflict market conditions. Looking ahead, OPEC+ is set to convene on 29 November, after seven member nations opted to hold September production targets steady through December. Because multiple Gulf producers are currently extracting below these set allocations, near-term crude tanker demand will hinge more heavily on real export output than on nominal production limits. For the VLCC sector specifically, any rebound in Gulf cargo availability must be weighed against a potential rise in effective ship availability as transit hurdles diminish. Key Takeaways The downward adjustment in VLCC freight rates paused towards the end of Week 47, despite lower weekly average earnings. VLCC net supply on the Arabian Gulf–China route exceeded October levels, while Arabian Gulf–China cargo volumes remained broadly unchanged and US Gulf–China shipments remained subdued. The decline in East of Suez earnings since early October remains considerably smaller than that recorded in the Atlantic, with the Hormuz risk premium still embedded in Gulf freight rates. The decline in East of Suez earnings since early October remains considerably smaller than that recorded in the Atlantic, suggesting that Hormuz-related risks continue to support Gulf freight rates. As geopolitical uncertainty increasingly forms part of prevailing market conditions, vessel availability relative to cargo demand appears to be exerting a greater influence on freight rate movements. Source: By Maria Bertzeletou · Senior Market Analyst, Signal, https://www.thesignalgroup.com/weekly-market-monitor/weekly-tanker-market-monitor-week-47-2026 2026-11-27 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: Greek-Owned Fleet Retains Global Lead, While Greek Flag Remains Outside the Top Five
articles.summary: Greece maintained its position as the world’s leading shipowning nation in 2025, accounting for 15.8 per cent of global shipping capacity, according to the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) Review of Maritime Transport 2026. The Greek-owned fleet totalled 5,168 vessels, with a combined...
articles.body: Greek-Owned Fleet Retains Global Lead, While Greek Flag Remains Outside the Top Five in Hellenic Shipping News 27/11/2026 G reece maintained its position as the world’s leading shipowning nation in 2025, accounting for 15.8 per cent of global shipping capacity, according to the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) Review of Maritime Transport 2026. The Greek-owned fleet totalled 5,168 vessels, with a combined carrying capacity of approximately 397.1 million deadweight tons (dwt), consolidating the country’s leading position in the international maritime industry. China ranked second, with a 15.0 per cent share of global capacity, followed by Japan (9.7 per cent), Singapore (7.3 per cent) and Hong Kong, China (4.9 per cent). Together, these five countries controlled 52.7 per cent of the world’s shipping capacity, highlighting the considerable concentration of global ship ownership. The UNCTAD figures, referring to 1 January 2026, show that Greece’s fleet remains substantially larger in terms of carrying capacity than those of its closest competitors. Its 397.1 million dwt compare with 377.0 million dwt for China and 243.2 million dwt for Japan. The Greek-owned fleet comprises 5,168 vessels, of which 4,606 are registered under foreign flags and just 553 under the Greek flag. Consequently, 88.3 per cent of Greek-owned shipping capacity is registered outside Greece, reflecting the international character of the country’s shipping industry. The figures underline an important characteristic of Greek shipping: although China operates a significantly larger number of vessels, the average carrying capacity of Greek-owned ships is considerably higher. Greece’s position is therefore particularly strong when measured by the total deadweight capacity of its fleet. The concentration of ownership also extends beyond the leading five. The top 10 shipowning economies account for 67 per cent of global shipping capacity, while the top 35 control 92.4 per cent. The Greek flag: Ninth globally, with a declining fleet In contrast to Greece’s dominant position in ship ownership, the national flag has a considerably smaller presence in international shipping. According to UNCTAD, the Greek flag ranked ninth worldwide on 1 January 2026, with 1,170 registered vessels and a combined capacity of 51.67 million dwt. This represented 2.0 per cent of global shipping capacity. Furthermore, the Greek-flagged fleet recorded a 3.3 per cent decline in deadweight capacity compared with the previous year, placing it among the flags that experienced a contraction during the period. The leading flag States were Liberia, Panama and the Marshall Islands, which together accounted for 44.1 per cent of global shipping capacity. Singapore and Hong Kong, China, completed the top five. The Greek flag, by comparison, had 1,170 vessels, representing 1.0 per cent of the global fleet by vessel count, and 2.0 per cent by carrying capacity. Its average vessel size stood at approximately 44,162 dwt. The gap between Greece’s position in ship ownership and its ranking in flag registration reflects a defining characteristic of international shipping. Shipowners frequently register their vessels in jurisdictions other than their home country, taking into account factors such as operating costs, taxation, regulatory frameworks, services and the reputation of the relevant registry. UNCTAD estimates that approximately 68.4 per cent of global shipping capacity is registered under a foreign flag, meaning that the country of registration differs from the country of ownership. The distinction is also evident in the value of the global fleet. Greece ranks second worldwide in terms of vessel value, accounting for 11.0 per cent of the total, behind China (12.6 per cent) and ahead of Japan (9.6 per cent). By contrast, the Greek flag accounts for just 1.7 per cent of global fleet value, ranking ninth among flag States. Overall, the figures confirm Greece’s enduring strength as a global maritime power, while highlighting the considerable difference between the international reach of Greek shipowners and the comparatively limited share of vessels operating under the national flag. articles.title: Global maritime trade set to stall in 2026 amid shipping disruptions and trade uncertainty
articles.summary: Global maritime trade is expected to stagnate in 2026 amid disruptions to major shipping routes and chokepoints, as well as wider trade uncertainty, according to the Review of Maritime Transport 2026, released by UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD). Disruptions across major shipping routes and chokepoints have forced...
articles.body: Global maritime trade set to stall in 2026 amid shipping disruptions and trade uncertainty in International Shipping News 27/11/2026 G lobal maritime trade is expected to stagnate in 2026 amid disruptions to major shipping routes and chokepoints, as well as wider trade uncertainty, according to the Review of Maritime Transport 2026, released by UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD). Disruptions across major shipping routes and chokepoints have forced vessels onto longer journeys, extending transit times, increasing fuel costs, driving port congestion and adding to uncertainty. Alternative ports, inland transport networks and logistics arrangements have helped keep trade moving, but at a higher cost. Seaborne trade reached 12.3 billion tons in 2025, up 1.9%, compared with 3.9% in 2024. UNCTAD projects zero growth in 2026, followed by a projected recovery of 3.2% in 2027. Containerized trade is expected to grow by 3.3% in 2026, outperforming overall maritime trade but slowing compared with 2025. Although growth in maritime trade volumes is projected to remain flat in 2026, maritime transport demand measured in ton-miles is expected to increase by 1.5%, reflecting longer voyages. The report calls for a shift from crisis response to embedded preparedness and adaptability, with “resilience by design and sustainability by default” guiding investment, planning, and operations. “Resilience by design and sustainability by default set the standard: maritime transport that keeps essential goods moving to every port, from the busiest hub to the most remote island,” says UNCTAD Acting Secretary-General Pedro Manuel Moreno. Major shipping routes and chokepoints under strain Conflict in the Middle East since late February 2026 has severely curtailed traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a gateway for around one fifth of global oil supplies and for other strategic commodities, including fertilizers. Before the disruption, around 120 ships crossed the strait daily. By early March, traffic measured by gross tonnage had fallen by roughly 95%. More than 20,000 seafarers were initially stranded in the Persian Gulf, with thousands remaining there for months. Instability in the Red Sea has kept many vessels on the longer route around the Cape of Good Hope, despite some liner operators returning to the corridor. Black Sea grain shipments remain exposed to security risks, while restrictions and changing traffic patterns have affected Panama Canal operations. Together, these disruptions affect trade in oil and gas, grain and food products, fertilizers and industrial inputs such as petrochemicals and aluminum. Their impact extends beyond shipping, affecting production costs and the availability of essential imports, particularly in countries dependent on imported food and energy. Higher costs hit vulnerable economies hardest Freight rates remained volatile through 2025 and 2026. Container spot rates more than doubled between January and August 2026, while crude oil tanker rates reached record highs on some routes. The report estimates that a sustained 70–80% increase in maritime fuel costs, compared with pre-disruption levels in January-February 2026, would raise consumer prices by 0.19% globally, 0.27% in small island developing states and 0.35% in least developed countries. These economies are particularly vulnerable because they have fewer shipping connections, fewer alternatives for sourcing imports and less capacity to absorb additional costs. Higher freight costs can add to existing pressures on households and businesses. Building resilience before the next shock Ports face growing congestion as vessel waiting times increase and shipping routes and port call patterns change. At the same time, they need to invest in digital systems, cybersecurity and climate-resilient infrastructure. The cargo-carrying capacity of the global shipping fleet expanded by 3.5% in 2025, outpacing maritime trade growth, yet 42% of vessels are more than 20 years old. Fleet renewal and efficient ships can help cut emissions and exposure to volatile fossil fuel prices. But uncertainty over future fuels and regulations risks delaying investment. Resilience by design means integrating resilience criteria at early stages of planning and decision-making. Sustainability by default means the integration of sustainability principles (economic, social, and environmental) becomes the norm. The report also stresses freedom of navigation and transit under international law, and protection of seafarers. Policy priorities ahead Developing countries need affordable finance, technology, skills and fit for purpose regulatory frameworks to make the transition to more sustainable shipping without losing trade competitiveness. UNCTAD calls on governments, industry and development partners to: • Plan alternative routes and logistics arrangements before disruptions occur, and strengthen preparedness for disruptions to essential food import. • Invest in efficient, well-connected, sustainable and climate-resilient ports and transport networks, and strengthen trade facilitation. • Support cleaner fleets and fuels through predictable rules and affordable finance. • Use digital tools and data to improve operational efficiency, performance tracking and measurement, and supply chain visibility, while strengthening cybersecurity and developing workforce skills. • Monitor freight markets trends and transport costs, and help vulnerable economies manage their impact. • Promoting sustainable shipping through accession to new international legal instruments and by strengthening the international maritime legal framework and its implementation, as necessary, to ensure it remains fit for purpose amid technological and operational changes. Source: UNCTAD Tops 2026-11-27 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: Disruptions across major shipping routes and chokepoints have forced vessels onto longer journeys, extending transit times, increasing fuel costs, driving port congestion and adding to uncertainty.
Alternative ports, inland transport networks and logistics arrangements have helped keep trade moving, but at a higher cost.
Seaborne trade reached 12.3 billion tons in 2025, up 1.9%, compared with 3.9% in 2024.

articles.title: Global shipping’s changing map: Where trade connections are growing and vulnerabilities are deepening
articles.summary: Global maritime trade is being reshaped by geopolitical tensions, changing production networks and shifting shipping routes. In the 2026 Review of Maritime Transport, UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD) examines how these changes are affecting developing regions. The report highlights a rising number of ship visits at...
articles.body: Global shipping’s changing map: Where trade connections are growing and vulnerabilities are deepening in International Shipping News 27/11/2026 Global maritime trade is being reshaped by geopolitical tensions, changing production networks and shifting shipping routes. In the 2026 Review of Maritime Transport, UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD) examines how these changes are affecting developing regions. The report highlights a rising number of ship visits at African ports, an increase in the average sizes of containerships calling at some of these ports; Asia’s continued strong shipping connectivity; and the impact of disruptions on maritime transport and trade. African ports on the front line of shifting trade routes Between the first half of 2018 and the second half of 2025, port calls by containerships in Africa increased by 30% and oil tanker calls by 85% – the fastest growth for these vessel types across regions. The expansion was partly driven by growing trade, particularly continued hydrocarbon exports, as well as investment in port infrastructure and the development of regional transshipment hubs. Changes in shipping routes have also been a factor. Disruptions in the Red Sea since late 2023 have prompted vessels travelling between Asia, Europe and across the Atlantic s to reroute around the Cape of Good Hope, bringing additional traffic to some African ports. Asia continues to lead in shipping connectivity Asia remains central to global container shipping networks, with China topping the UNCTAD Liner Shipping Connectivity Index in June 2026. Viet Nam has made particularly strong gains, with its connectivity increasing more than fourfold over the past two decades. It ranked sixth on the index in June 2026, up from 28th in February 2006. The jump largely reflects a substantial increase in deployed annual shipping capacity and the use of larger vessels, alongside Viet Nam’s growing role as a manufacturing and export hub. New disruptions in 2026 add pressure on shipping, ports and inland transport Disruptions to operations in the Strait of Hormuz have caused a decline in global oil tanker port calls between June 2025 and June 2026. Meanwhile, insurance costs, surcharges and freight rates have risen, and congestion has increased at ports receiving rerouted traffic. Liner shipping connectivity was also affected. Economies in the conflict-affected region recorded sharp falls in the Liner Shipping Connectivity Index, with the largest reaching 65 %, as liner carriers suspended services and rerouted vessels, reducing deployed shipping capacity on some Middle East-linked routes. Operational challenges in the Panama Canal, amid drought risks, have added to the complexity. From observed resilience to structural resilience Maritime trade in 2025 and early 2026 displayed observed resilience, with cargo continuing to move or being redirected in response to disruptions. But the report cautions that this is not the same as structural resilience, which depends on whether routes, suppliers and logistics arrangements can be adjusted without disproportionate costs or prolonged loss of access. “The continued movement and redirection of cargo demonstrate observed resilience, but also entailed longer routes, higher costs and greater operational complexity, revealing that structural resilience remains uneven,” the report underscores. With the outlook being shaped by uncertainty and ongoing disruption, the report calls for a shift from merely reacting to shocks towards “resilience by design”, embedding structural resilience into transport systems. Proactive risk monitoring, assessment and management, along with contingency planning, viable alternative routes and logistics systems will be crucial. Stronger coordination among ports and transport corridors will remain essential. Together, these measures will help ensure operational and business continuity, as well as uninterrupted, reliable and affordable access to global markets amid disruptions. Source: UNCTAD 2026-11-27 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

As a result, year to date, crude oil and dirty-product cargo volumes are down 5% on last year, ...
articles.body: Tanker Shipping Market Overview & Outlook: Disruptions still dominate tanker market outlook in International Shipping News 27/11/2026 “T his year, tanker markets have been affected by disruption to transits through the Strait of Hormuz, the Houthi blockade of Saudi Arabian Red Sea exports, and attacks on Russian refineries and on ships in the Black Sea. As a result, year to date, crude oil and dirty-product cargo volumes are down 5% on last year, while clean-product cargo volumes are down 11%,” says Niels Rasmussen, Chief Shipping Analyst at BIMCO. Since the start of the third quarter, however, ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman from shuttles crossing the Strait of Hormuz have increased significantly. Over the past four weeks, Middle East tanker exports have reached 75% of pre-war levels, even though Saudi Arabian Red Sea exports have fallen since the Houthi blockade began. Russian clean-product exports have meanwhile averaged 58% below last year’s level since the start of the third quarter, because of Ukrainian attacks on refineries. “Despite lower volumes, risk premiums and reduced fleet efficiency have pushed freight rates to unprecedented levels. Rates have, however, recently weakened, and Platts S&P Global Energy’s Global Dirty Tanker Index and Global Clean Tanker Index are now 25%–30% below their October peaks,” says Rasmussen. For 2027 and 2028, two scenarios are presented: “SoH closed” and “SoH open”. They differ in how three situations develop: the Strait of Hormuz, the threat to Saudi Arabian Red Sea exports and the attacks affecting Russian exports. “SoH closed” assumes that these disruptions stay unchanged, while “SoH open” assumes that all three are resolved gradually during 2027. In “SoH open”, we expect strong growth in crude tanker ship demand in 2027, driven by a global oil oversupply. Trade patterns are expected to gradually return to normal, which should lead to longer sailing distances and support further demand growth in 2028. Global refinery throughput is expected to grow more slowly than oil supply, so we expect product tanker ship demand to grow more slowly. Shorter sailing distances could even cause demand to fall in 2028. In “SoH closed”, there is little room for cargo volume growth, although the higher Persian Gulf exports seen in the second half of 2026 are assumed to continue. The shorter sailing distances seen in the same period are also expected to continue, which would reduce ship demand. “In our “SoH open” scenario, we expect both crude tanker and product tanker freight rates to ease as risk premiums fade and ship supply grows. In our “SoH closed” scenario, we expect ship supply to grow faster than ship demand in both years, so freight rates should also weaken, but could remain higher than in the “SoH open” scenario as risk premiums should remain. It is very uncertain, however, when and how quickly the disruptions will ease,” concludes Rasmussen. Source: BIMCO Tops 2026-11-27 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: Baltic Dry Index Up for 4th Day in Dry Bulk Market , International Shipping News 27/11/2026 The Baltic Exchange’s dry bulk freight index, which tracks rates for ships carrying dry bulk commodities, advanced for a fourth straight session on Thursday, rising by 1.5% to its highest level since September 29 at 3,152 points. The gains reflect tighter vessel availability and stronger demand for shipping capacity, particularly for capesize vessels, with rates in this segment climbing nearly 13% over the week. Higher iron ore shipments from Australia and Brazil to China, alongside seasonal restocking ahead of winter, have supported cargo demand. Guinea has also contributed to the increase, with rising bauxite exports and growing iron ore shipments following the ramp-up of the Simandou project. Meanwhile, the panamax index, which usually carries 60,000 to 70,000 tons of coal or grain, rose by 2.2% to its highest since October 19 at 2,273 points. Among smaller vessels, the supramax index went up 0.2% to 1,816 points. Source: Trading Economics 2026-11-27 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

Xeneta analyst insight – US shippers still feeling the most pain despite further rate increases expected into Europe in December Peter Sand, Xeneta Chief Analyst: “There are contrasting fortunes across Far East fronthauls into Europe and the US, but the implications for shippers vary dramatically depending on your perspective. “Early Xeneta data indicates average spot rates to Mediterranean will increase a further 10-15% at the start of December, having already increased 27% since 14 October. articles.title: Open letter on freedom of navigation and the protection of seafarers
articles.summary: European Shipowners | ECSA, BIMCO, the Cruise Lines International Association (CLIA), the International Chamber of Shipping (ICS), INTERCARGO, INTERFERRY, INTERTANKO and the World Shipping Council (WSC) welcome and support the EU-led ‘Pledge on Maintaining the Integrity of the International Law of the Sea – No...
articles.body: Open letter on freedom of navigation and the protection of seafarers in International Shipping News 27/11/2026 European Shipowners | ECSA, BIMCO, the Cruise Lines International Association (CLIA), the International Chamber of Shipping (ICS), INTERCARGO, INTERFERRY, INTERTANKO and the World Shipping Council (WSC) welcome and support the EU-led ‘Pledge on Maintaining the Integrity of the International Law of the Sea – No Fees/No Tolls’, announced on 12 October 2026. We commend the European Union, its Member States and partner countries for their united commitment to protecting freedom of navigation, which underpins global shipping and the carriage of around 90% of world trade. The pledge sends an important signal of international unity against the use of tolls or fees and restrictions affecting passage through straits used for international navigation. We share its commitment to preserving the legal framework established by the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), rejecting coercive unilateral measures and strengthening multilateral cooperation, particularly through the International Maritime Organization (IMO). For our industry, the safety and protection of seafarers is a precondition of freedom of navigation. Seafarers are the backbone of global trade and must be able to carry out their work safely. They must never become targets of violence. Their safety and welfare must remain at the centre of international efforts to safeguard maritime routes. Seafarers have already suffered injuries and lost their lives while carrying out their essential work. We therefore particularly welcome the pledge’s support for non-escalatory multilateral initiatives. We urge the supporting countries to translate this commitment into sustained cooperation and practical measures to protect merchant ships and their crews, while keeping essential trade moving safely. Such efforts should be accompanied by sustained coordination between States, relevant naval forces and the shipping industry to help translate commitments to freedom of navigation into effective protection of seafarers and shipping at sea. As our industry has previously underlined in relation to the Strait of Hormuz, compulsory transit charges, including service fees that in practice amount to tolls, would set a deeply worrying precedent. Freedom of navigation is fundamental to the welfare of people worldwide and to the global economy, underpinning the free flow of trade, energy security and the supply of critical materials. We urge governments to uphold these rights consistently and resist attempts to make their exercise conditional on payment. The consequences of disrupted shipping reach far beyond our industry. Reliable maritime transport supports the security of supply of food, energy and essential goods, and underpins economies worldwide. Protecting the people who deliver these goods is a shared international responsibility. We therefore encourage additional countries to support the pledge and stand ready to work with its supporters, the IMO and the wider international community to advance its objectives. Together, we must ensure that freedom of navigation is upheld in practice and that seafarers can perform their essential work without fear for their lives. articles.body: ENGINE: Americas Bunker Fuel Availability Outlook in International Shipping News 27/11/2026 North America Bunker demand in Houston is strong and prompt availability is tight across all three grades, a trader said. HSFO and VLSFO require lead times of 6-8 days, and most suppliers can deliver LSMGO within 4-5 days this week. High winds and rough seas are occasionally disrupting supply by restricting the movement of bunker barges and their reloading. Fog season is under way on the US Gulf Coast and could disrupt and intermittently close the Houston Ship Channel, the waterway linking the port to the open sea, until March, a source said. Sea fog could cut visibility at US Gulf Coast ports from this weekend, according to weather data provider DTN. The threat is most widespread on Sunday, when it is moderate in Galveston, Freeport, Port Arthur, Corpus Christi, Lake Charles, Marsh Island, Port Fourchon, Venice, New Orleans and Mobile Bay. Tampa and Pascagoula face a moderate threat on Monday, and the threat is expected to stay low in Brownsville. Suppliers are delivering on a first-come, first-served basis at the Galveston Offshore Lightering Area (GOLA). The anchorage is congested and availability is tight, with most suppliers needing lead times of more than a week for all three grades, a trader tells ENGINE. Bunker demand in New York has been steady, and weather disruptions are now expected to cause delays and lengthen lead times, a trader said. Current lead times are around 5-6 days for LSMGO, around 6-7 days for HSFO and 7-8 days for VLSFO. A storm warning is in effect in New York until late Thursday night. Sandy Hook Pilots, the association whose pilots guide ships into and out of the port, has suspended services after the forecast storm window widened, ship agent Moran Shipping Agencies said. Most large ships need a pilot to enter or leave the port, so the suspension halts their arrivals and departures. The last departure was allowed at 03.00 EST (08.00 GMT) on Thursday and the last arrival at 07.00 EST (12.00 GMT). Pilots expect to resume with departures from 05.00 EST (10.00 GMT) on Friday and arrivals from 09.00 EST (14.00 GMT), but Moran said the restart is likely to be pushed back by around four hours and will be confirmed later. On the US West Coast, bunker demand and prices are both high in Los Angeles and Long Beach. Availability is tight for HSFO, VLSFO and LSMGO, and suppliers are recommending lead times of more than a week and up to 10 days. HSFO in Los Angeles has traded at a premium to VLSFO in Houston since 15 September, according to ENGINE data, bucking the usual price relationship between the two grades. HSFO, which is typically cheaper than VLSFO and used by vessels fitted with scrubbers, has maintained the premium for much of this period. The premium peaked at $151/mt on 19 October but has narrowed over the course of this month. Los Angeles HSFO briefly traded below Houston VLSFO between 21 and 24 November, before returning to a $16/mt premium on Wednesday. In Canada, suppliers in Vancouver can deliver VLSFO and LSMGO within four days. HSFO availability is somewhat tighter, and deliveries can require lead times of more than a week, a source said. Latin America and the Caribbean Bunker availability is tight in Panama. At the port of Balboa, on the Pacific side of the Panama Canal, most suppliers need lead times of 8-11 days to deliver VLSFO and HSFO. LSMGO can be secured within 5-7 days. In Colombia, availability is good in Cartagena, Barranquilla and Santa Marta, a source said. Suppliers at all three ports can deliver VLSFO and LSMGO within 3-4 days. HSFO is tight in Cartagena and available only on prior consultation. In Peru, VLSFO and LSMGO availability is normal in Callao, with lead times of 3-7 days, a source said. HSFO is tight, and the earliest date suppliers can deliver it is 3 December. In Brazil, availability of all three grades is normal in Rio de Janeiro, with lead times of 3-7 days, a source said. VLSFO and LSMGO availability is also normal in Santos and in the northern ports of Belem and Vila do Conde, with the same lead times. HSFO is not on offer in Santos, Belem or Vila do Conde, or in the southern ports of Paranagua and Rio Grande. VLSFO and LSMGO availability is tightening in Paranagua, and the earliest delivery date for both grades in Rio Grande is 30 November. Rough weather is disrupting bunker operations in Zona Comun, the anchorage on the River Plate shared by Argentina and Uruguay, a source said. Deliveries are continuing despite the disruption, and VLSFO availability remains tight, with recommended lead times of 8-12 days. LSMGO availability is also tight, another source said. Source: By Gautamee Hazarika, ENGINE, https://www.engine.online/news 2026-11-27 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: GPS Jamming Resilience: See Where AIS Positions Are Denied or Injected in Near Real Time
articles.summary: GPS Jamming Is Something That Happens to an Area GPS jamming is not a vessel doing something. It is outside interference, usually from a military source, affecting everything in range. Any vessel, aircraft, or phone in that area is hit regardless of flag, owner, or cargo. articles.body: GPS Jamming Resilience: See Where AIS Positions Are Denied or Injected in Near Real Time in International Shipping News 27/11/2026 GPS Jamming Is Something That Happens to an Area GPS jamming is not a vessel doing something. It is outside interference, usually from a military source, affecting everything in range. Any vessel, aircraft, or phone in that area is hit regardless of flag, owner, or cargo. That makes it different from deliberate manipulation, where a vessel alters its own reported position. GPS jamming is indiscriminate. A clean vessel and a sanctioned one in the same waters are both exposed, though how each is affected depends on its equipment. It shows up in AIS in two ways: • Denied: The transmission is blocked. Tracking degrades or disappears, and you cannot see where the vessel is or what it is doing. • Injected: The positional coordinates are overwritten. The vessel appears somewhere it is not, sometimes next to a port, sometimes alongside other vessels it never met. The shapes give it away. GPS jamming around the UAE throws vessels into near-perfect circles. The Black Sea produces repeating triangles, with vessels displaced between the same two points again and again. Real traffic does not move like that, which is how an injected position is distinguished from a real one. Injected AIS positions near Lesser Tunb pull vessel tracks into a tight loop around a single point, a pattern real traffic does not make. Source: Windward Maritime AI™ Platform. Denied is the harder problem. An injected position leaves a pattern you can recognize. A gap leaves nothing to read. The Scale In the Middle East Gulf alone, since February 28, 2026, Windward has recorded 94,804 unique vessels affected by GPS jamming and more than 3.1 million false ship-to-ship meetings generated by injected coordinates. GPS jamming concentrates in conflict zones and chokepoints. The Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb account for the largest share, followed closely by the Black Sea around Crimea and Novorossiysk, then the Baltic and the northern Caspian. The Middle East Gulf and Strait of Hormuz sit behind those but remain persistent. What the Map Shows Windward’s GPS Jamming Resilience active heatmap gives you three things that a general warning does not. 1. Whether the signal is denied or injected. A denial signal tells you whether a period of dark activity should be treated as suspicious or cleared. An injected position tells you a port call or a war zone visit may never have happened. 2. How confident the call is. Areas carry high, medium, or low confidence, so you know how much weight to put on what you are seeing. 3. Where a displaced vessel came from. Click an injection area, and you can trace back to where the vessel actually was. That is the detail that turns a false position into a usable one. Latency is about 90 minutes, calculated across the whole map. The timeline slider runs back 90 days, so you can see patterns and where the GPS jamming hotspots are. False Ship-to-Ship Meetings Are Suppressed Automatically GPS jamming does not only hide vessels. It invents activity that never happened. Injected coordinates place vessels alongside each other when no meeting took place, and those false meetings land on a compliance team as alerts. The volumes involved are substantial. In the six days from February 28 to March 5, 2026, as GPS jamming in the Gulf intensified, Windward removed 2,056 port calls across 845 vessels and 20,848 meetings across 695 vessels. None of them happened. Since June, this has been automated. Up to 99% of false ship-to-ship meetings are identified and suppressed before they ever reach the platform, so they never appear on a timeline and never generate an alert. For a compliance team working a high-volume book, that is noise removed at the source rather than cleared afterward. What Teams Are Using It For Clearing Compliance Risk A dark activity on a vessel timeline is ambiguous on its own. Checked against the GPS jamming history for that time and place, it often resolves immediately. This is the primary value for compliance teams. In October 2026, more than 700 vessels in the Black Sea appeared at Callao, Peru, thousands of miles from where they actually were. The model flagged spoofed positions around Callao across 18 days, peaking between October 9 and 11, and linked them back to the areas off Romania and Bulgaria where the vessels really were. Without that link, a screening system records 700 vessels calling in Peru. Callao displacement linked back to Black Sea positions, October 2026. Source: Windward Maritime AI™ Platform. Keeping Due Diligence Standards Intact Some companies have quietly relaxed scrutiny in heavily jammed regions, because chasing every alert means going back to clients repeatedly over events that turn out to be interference. Visibility into where GPS jamming actually occurred lets them keep the standard and ask the question only when it is warranted. The alternative is an internal rule that alerts from a whole region can be disregarded. That clears the queue and removes the real findings along with the false ones. Planning Routes Safety teams can see which routes have been jammed historically and route around them, or warn crews already underway to switch to alternative navigation methods before entering an affected zone. The Red Sea pattern shows why history matters more than a live check. Jamming there runs on a schedule, largely absent from 06:00 UTC until around 15:00, then heavy. A vessel’s transit time through that corridor determines whether it is affected at all. Share of injected jamming by hour of day in the Red Sea, showing a consistent daily schedule. Source: Windward Maritime AI™ Platform. Share of injected jamming by hour of day in the Red Sea, showing a consistent daily schedule. Source: Windward Maritime AI™ Platform. Assessing Voyage Security GPS jamming starting in an area can indicate an incoming threat or military activity. For security teams monitoring a voyage through a chokepoint, that is worth knowing in near real time. The correlation is visible in the data. In the Middle East Gulf through Q3 2026, jamming spiked with each U.S. strike on Iran. The September 1 strike produced 1,699 incidents in a single day against a regional average of 315, and set the global quarterly peak of 6,838 the same day. On September 1, 2026, the day of a U.S. strike on Iran, Windward’s GPS jamming heatmap shows injection across the Middle East Gulf. Clicking an area shows its confidence level. Source: Windward Maritime AI™ Platform. Protecting Subsea Assets Sending a maintenance crew offshore is expensive and slow to arrange. If GPS is denied over the cable route when they arrive, they cannot locate the cable, and the deployment is wasted. Knowing where jamming has been active, and when, lets operators plan deployments around it rather than discovering the problem on site. The same history is worth considering at the design stage. A cable route that runs through a persistently jammed corridor will be harder to maintain for its entire service life. The Pattern Itself Is Intelligence GPS jamming data is useful beyond cleaning up other records. Where it happens, when, in what shape, and how that changes over time is a finding in its own right. What the 90 days show is that a lot of it is deliberate and structured. The Red Sea runs to a daily schedule. The Black Sea repeats the same displacement patterns between the same points. In the Gulf, GPS jamming spiked alongside each U.S. strike on Iran through Q3. Patterns that are regular are decisions. Someone is choosing where and when, and the map is the record of those choices. That is visible from the map and from nowhere else. A single vessel’s track shows interference. Ninety days of global coverage shows intent. Source: Windward 2026-11-27 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: It is outside interference, usually from a military source, affecting everything in range.
Any vessel, aircraft, or phone in that area is hit regardless of flag, owner, or cargo.
That makes it different from deliberate manipulation, where a vessel alters its own reported position.

articles.title: Marlink appoints Greg Hyttenrauch as new CEO

articles.body: Marlink has appointed Greg Hyttenrauch as its new Chief Executive Officer, effective 1 January 2027, as the maritime connectivity and digital services provider prepares for a leadership transition after more than two decades under Erik Ceuppens. Hyttenrauch will succeed Ceuppens, who is moving to the position of Chairman of the Board after 22 years leading the company. In his new role, Ceuppens will remain involved in Marlink’s strategic direction, working alongside the incoming CEO and the board as the business continues to expand its connectivity, cybersecurity and managed digital services. The appointment brings an executive with more than 30 years of experience in technology, telecommunications and managed services to Marlink. Hyttenrauch currently leads the €2 billion cloud and security services business at Deutsche Telekom’s T-Systems, where he oversees approximately 10,000 employees. His previous positions include senior leadership roles at Cognizant, Vodafone, Capgemini, CSC and EDS, with experience in managing international technology businesses and integrating cloud, security and digital services. Leadership transition after 22 years During Ceuppens’ tenure, Marlink expanded from a satellite communications provider into an international managed services business serving maritime, energy, enterprise and government customers. The company now employs approximately 1,700 people worldwide, with its services extending across satellite connectivity, network management, cybersecurity, cloud and industrial digital technologies. The incoming CEO will be responsible for overseeing Marlink’s global operations and growth strategy, including the continued development of its connectivity and digital services portfolio. “Erik and the team have built a fantastic global company and I am honoured to have the opportunity to lead it into its next phase of growth,” said Greg Hyttenrauch, incoming CEO of Marlink. Ceuppens welcomed the appointment, highlighting Hyttenrauch’s experience in international managed services and the company’s plans for further development. “In Greg we have found a leader with entrepreneurial spirit and extensive experience in building international managed service businesses, combining connectivity, cybersecurity, cloud and digital technologies,” said Erik Ceuppens, outgoing CEO and incoming Chairman of Marlink. The transition will take effect at the beginning of 2027, with Hyttenrauch assuming responsibility for Marlink’s next phase of development while Ceuppens continues to support the business at board level.

articles.title: The absurdity of ‘competitive’ salaries
articles.summary: Maritime recruitment could benefit from the same commercial transparency that shipping demands of almost every other aspect of its business. Mike Darby from Merchant Recruitment explains. Imagine if the shipping industry operated the same way as its job adverts. “How much for VLSFO in Rotterdam?” “Competitive.”...
articles.body: Contributions Operations The absurdity of ‘competitive’ salaries Splash November 27, 2026 0 1 2 minutes read Maritime recruitment could benefit from the same commercial transparency that shipping demands of almost every other aspect of its business. Mike Darby from Merchant Recruitment explains. Imagine if the shipping industry operated the same way as its job adverts. “How much for VLSFO in Rotterdam?” “Competitive.” “Okay, but what’s the price?” “Confidential.” “What are owners looking for on the freight?” “Dependent on experience.” “Can you give me an indication?” “We’d prefer to understand your current freight rate first.” It sounds ridiculous, doesn’t it? Yet when it comes to recruitment, this is an approach we’ve somehow accepted as perfectly normal. Shipping is an industry built around commercial information. We track freight rates, bunker prices, vessel values and market movements with extraordinary attention to detail. Entire businesses exist to provide transparency around what things cost. Yet when it comes to one of the most important investments a company makes, its people, we’re remarkably reluctant to discuss the numbers. “Salary: Competitive.” Two words that appear in countless job advertisements and tell potential applicants absolutely nothing. Imagine listing your house on Rightmove for “£Competitive, dependent on the buyer’s current mortgage.” You probably wouldn’t get many serious enquiries. Yet every day, shipping companies advertise opportunities that might require someone to change employer, relocate their family or move halfway around the world, without giving them any indication of what they’ll actually earn. Of course, there are legitimate reasons why salaries aren’t always advertised. I’ve recruited for positions where internal sensitivities, varying levels of experience or genuine confidentiality have made publishing a figure difficult. Sometimes an employer is willing to consider candidates at several levels of seniority, meaning the salary could vary significantly depending on who they hire. As recruiters, we’re not entirely innocent either. We’ve all advertised positions without salary information, myself included. However, I struggle to believe that every position advertised as “competitive” falls into one of these categories. The reality is that employers generally have a budget in mind. They know roughly what they’re prepared to pay, even if there’s some flexibility for an exceptional candidate. So why not share it? A salary range doesn’t have to be a promise. It’s a starting point for a conversation. £60,000 to £80,000 tells a candidate whether an opportunity is broadly aligned with their expectations. “Competitive” tells them nothing. It also makes the recruitment process more efficient. There’s little benefit in spending weeks interviewing an experienced ship operator expecting £90,000 when the employer’s budget is £60,000. Both parties could have established that within the first conversation. There’s also a wider issue around trust. When the first question a candidate receives is “What’s your current salary?” but the employer isn’t prepared to disclose what they’re offering, the conversation immediately feels one-sided. Surely recruitment should be about establishing someone’s value in the market and the responsibilities of the position, rather than simply calculating the smallest increase required to persuade them to move. I don’t believe every shipping company needs to publish an exact salary for every vacancy. There will always be exceptions, particularly for confidential or senior appointments, but providing a realistic range, whether publicly or during an initial conversation, seems like a reasonable expectation. If confidentiality genuinely prevents that, explain why. We’re an industry that can tell you the daily movement of freight rates across multiple vessel classes and trade routes. Surely we can give someone a reasonable indication of what they’ll earn before asking them to change their life. That doesn’t seem particularly revolutionary. It just seems fair. articles.summary: Chinese shipbuilders are scheduled to deliver more than three times as much bulk carrier and tanker tonnage in 2028 as they did last year, according to fresh research from Banchero Costa that raises further questions over the industry’s ability to make good on its record orderbook. articles.body: Greater China Shipyards China faces daunting shipbuilding arithmetic Sam Chambers November 27, 2026 0 36 2 minutes read Hengli Hengli Chinese shipbuilders are scheduled to deliver more than three times as much bulk carrier and tanker tonnage in 2028 as they did last year, according to fresh research from Banchero Costa that raises further questions over the industry’s ability to make good on its record orderbook. Chinese yards are contracted to deliver 92.7m dwt of bulk carriers and tankers in 2028, against just 30.4m dwt last year and a previous annual record of 62.6m dwt set in 2011. Across the seven principal merchant shipping sectors tracked by the Italian shipbroker, the orderbook stood at 5,488 vessels totalling 172.3m compensated gross tonnes (cgt) at the end of October, up 24% year-on-year and some 31% above the previous 2007 peak recorded in its dataset. The figures complement Clarksons Research’s broader assessment, reported by Splash earlier this month, which put the global newbuilding backlog at a record 226.1m cgt, worth approximately $700bn. Perhaps the most striking statistics in Banchero Costa’s latest outlook concern the proliferation of new and resuscitated shipyards. Some 106 yards that did not deliver a single vessel across the seven surveyed sectors between 2019 and 2023 now hold orders for 909 ships. These yards delivered just 1m cgt last year but are scheduled to deliver 10.1m cgt in 2028, representing one-sixth of anticipated global output across these sectors. At the centre of this extraordinary industrial expansion is Hengli. The Dalian shipbuilder, which only recommenced commercial deliveries in 2024, delivered 66 vessels in the opening 10 months of this year but is contracted to deliver 101 next year and an astonishing 193 in 2028. As reported by Splash earlier this month, research from Danish Ship Finance shows shipbuilding capacity has expanded by just 30% since 2020, while the orderbook has grown three and a half times. The Danish financier estimates that between 10m and 11m cgt of scheduled deliveries could slip annually from 2027 and 2028, with the highest-performing yards already booked at 164% of available capacity for 2028. Equipment availability remains another considerable headache. Speaking at last month’s Maritime CEO Forum in Monaco, Star Bulk’s Milena Pappas revealed that some prospective shipbuilders had even asked owners to source main engines themselves. With 55% of this year’s contracted tonnage now scheduled for delivery in 2029 or later, Banchero Costa expects ordering activity to slow heading into next year. For freight markets, the greatest risks lie in the container and crude tanker sectors, where scheduled deliveries in 2028 alone equate to 17.3% and 12% of their respective existing fleets. The extent of delivery slippage could ultimately prove one of the most important determinants of shipping’s earnings over the remainder of this decade. articles.body: Port operators and the ILWU Local 26 watchmen union arrived at a last-minute agreement Friday night averting a labor disruption at the ports of LA and Long Beach. The new agreement – which should be welcomed by the many shippers still working to move holiday inventories inland – remains tentative until ratification, but the union will continue working under its expired contract until it votes. Last week’s Trump-Xi summit ended with calls for stability in the trade relationship, and China has taken additional conciliatory steps since then. Nonetheless, the sides are preparing optionsshould they become necessary, as the January 10th truce expiration approaches. The USTR may release the findings of its Section 301 investigations into excess manufacturing capacity practices by a list of countries including China as early as next week. Several of the countries targeted by the study have rejected the accusations. But as these new tariffs would likely only restore duties to IEEPA levels – which were agreed upon by the US and those trade partners last year – it is unclear whether or not some countries will view these steps as escalations and take retaliatory measures as a result. Even if findings are released soon however, the typical procedural next steps – a comments period followed by hearings – would likely mean a couple more months until the president could actually introduce tariffs based on the report. President Trump only enacted tariffs based on the most recent 301 investigation, which focused on issues of forced labor, eight weeks after the USTR released its report. Expectations of tariff increases may be among the several converging drivers of stronger than anticipated transpacific container volumes and the extended peak season over the last few months. Weather-driven congestion and capacity reductions may also have helped keep container rates higher for longer even as demand has cooled. But transpacific spot prices have finally started to ease on these lanes. Asia – N. America West Coast rates fell 6% to about $8,000/FEU last week, with daily rates so far this week down to $7,500/FEU, their lowest level since the end of August. East Coast prices were stable at $9,800/FEU but have slid to $9,000/FEU and back to July levels so far this week. But rates are still nearly three times higher than a year ago. Carriers are increasing blanked sailings as volumes cool, and with only a few weeks until pre-Lunar New Year demand kicks in, prices are still likely to be quite elevated when they start climbing again. Despite the post-peak, pre-LNY volume lull on Asia – Europe lanes, carrier GRIs are pushing rates up – at least for now. Asia – N. Europe prices dipped 1% last week but have climbed about $200/FEU so far this week to $3,500/FEU. Mediterranean rates spiked 20% to about $5,200/FEU last week and daily rates have so far increased another $300/FEU, though current market dynamics do make it possible that prices will backslide in the near term. When LNY demand does pick up though, some forwarders expect existing congestion in N. Europe to worsen, which will help put upward pressure on rates and could lead carriers to start rolling some contracted volumes again. In air cargo, seasonal demand is stacking on top of the surge in shipments needed for data center construction on some Far East – N. America lanes to push rates up with only about three weeks of peak season to go. Freightos Air Index South East Asia – N. America prices have climbed 15% to about $8.00/kg over the past month marking a 50% gain compared to last year. Far East – N. America rates cooled 9% last week to $8.40/kg with daily prices showing a further correction, possibly reflecting capacity additions as demand increases. China – Europe prices dipped 6% to $4.74/kg last week. This rate is just a 15% premium to last year as the lane is still adjusting to the sharp drop in e-commerce volumes since EU changes to de minimis this summer. Transatlantic rates climbed another 9% to an average of $3.56/kg last week and to its highest since June 2022. Europe-US peak season demand is likely combining with Asia-origin volumes seeking alternative routes to the US as long-haul space tightens. Winter schedules and freighter shifts to higher volume lanes may also be adding upward pressure on rates. Judah Levine, Head of Research, Freightos Group (Nasdaq: CRGO)

articles.title: Viking takes delivery of first hydrogen-powered cruise ship
articles.summary: Viking has taken delivery of Viking Libra, described as the world’s first hydrogen-powered cruise ship, following completion of construction at Fincantieri’s shipyard in Ancona, Italy. The handover on 25 November 2026 marks an important step in the introduction of hydrogen technology to the cruise sector. Measuring...
articles.body: Viking has taken delivery of Viking Libra, described as the world’s first hydrogen-powered cruise ship, following completion of construction at Fincantieri’s shipyard in Ancona, Italy. The handover on 25 November 2026 marks an important step in the introduction of hydrogen technology to the cruise sector. Measuring 239 metres in length and approximately 54,300 GT, Viking Libra can accommodate up to 998 passengers in 499 staterooms. Its propulsion and power generation systems incorporate liquefied hydrogen and fuel cells, enabling the vessel to operate without emissions when using its hydrogen-based systems. The technology has been developed to allow the ship to operate in environmentally sensitive areas where restrictions on emissions are particularly important. While hydrogen forms part of its power system, Viking Libra is not designed to rely exclusively on hydrogen for all operations. The delivery follows the vessel’s launch at Fincantieri’s Ancona shipyard in March 2026, when the ship entered the final stages of construction ahead of its planned introduction to Viking’s fleet. Export credit financing supports delivery The project was supported by export credit financing involving BNP Paribas and a syndicate of international banks, with backing from Italy’s export credit agency SACE and SIMEST. International law firm Norton Rose Fulbright advised the lenders on the original financing and subsequent delivery arrangements, with legal teams working across London and Milan. The transaction adds to the firm’s involvement in export credit-backed cruise ship financing, a market that continues to support investment in new vessels and emerging maritime technologies. With Viking Libra now delivered, Viking becomes the first cruise operator to introduce a vessel equipped with a liquefied hydrogen and fuel-cell system designed to enable zero-emission operation.

articles.title: SUARDIAZ adds 5,500-CEU car carrier to Atlantic Line

articles.body: SUARDIAZ Group has added the 5,500-CEU car carrier RS Atlantico to its Atlantic Line, increasing capacity for vehicle and rolling cargo shipments between Morocco and Europe. The vessel has arrived in Zeebrugge, Belgium, where the company marked its entry into service with an event attended by customers, partners and industry representatives. RS Atlantico joins three vessels already operating on the Atlantic Line, which connects Morocco, Spain, the United Kingdom, France and Belgium. The additional capacity will support automotive manufacturers using the route while enabling SUARDIAZ to accommodate a broader range of rolling cargo, including machinery and heavy equipment. The vessel measures 190 metres in length, has a gross tonnage of approximately 55,000 GT and is equipped with a dual-fuel propulsion system capable of operating on liquefied natural gas (LNG). Its design allows it to transport passenger vehicles alongside larger industrial cargo, providing additional flexibility for customers with different shipping requirements. The expansion forms part of SUARDIAZ Group’s wider investment in automotive logistics. Alongside its shipping operations, the company has developed its inland transport capabilities, with a fleet of more than 500 trucks and a new terminal in Liverpool. The addition of RS Atlantico strengthens the maritime side of this network, complementing the group’s existing investments in vehicle distribution and logistics infrastructure. “The addition of RS Atlantico to our Atlantic Line turns our ongoing investment strategy into operational capacity. For SUARDIAZ Group, growth is not simply about adding new assets, but about having greater capacity and better tools to support our customers in an increasingly global and demanding industry,” said Juan Riva, CEO of SUARDIAZ Group. The vessel’s arrival also highlights Zeebrugge’s role in SUARDIAZ’s European shipping network. As part of the Port of Antwerp-Bruges, the Belgian port provides access to major automotive markets and connections with the United Kingdom, making it an important point on the Atlantic Line. With the new vessel joining the existing fleet, SUARDIAZ is expanding its ability to serve automotive manufacturers and other customers moving rolling cargo between North Africa and Europe.

articles.title: Windcat orders second offshore support vessel from Damen
articles.summary: Windcat has signed a contract with Damen Shipyards Group for a second Multi-Purpose Accommodation Support Vessel (MP-ASV), expanding its Innovation Series programme to strengthen its capabilities in the offshore energy sector. The agreement, signed on 24 November 2026, follows an initial order placed a year earlier,...
articles.body: Windcat has signed a contract with Damen Shipyards Group for a second Multi-Purpose Accommodation Support Vessel (MP-ASV), expanding its Innovation Series programme to strengthen its capabilities in the offshore energy sector. The agreement, signed on 24 November 2026, follows an initial order placed a year earlier, which included options for five additional vessels. Developed jointly by Damen and Windcat, the Innovation Series builds on the companies’ experience with the Elevation Series of Commissioning Service Operations Vessels (CSOVs), combining offshore accommodation with equipment designed for a wider range of marine operations. The new MP-ASV will measure 102 metres in length and 20 metres in width, with 750 m² of deck space and 111 cabins accommodating up to 190 personnel. Its design allows it to support offshore wind projects, subsea cable repairs, remotely operated vehicle (ROV) activities and offshore accommodation requirements. For subsea operations, the vessel will be equipped with a crane capable of lifting 150 tonnes, which can also operate as a 15-tonne 3D motion-compensated crane. A motion-compensated gangway with interchangeable connection systems will provide access to offshore installations, while a DP2+ dynamic positioning system with additional thrusters will enhance operational redundancy. Focus on operational flexibility and efficiency The Innovation Series also incorporates technologies intended to improve energy efficiency and support the use of lower-emission fuels. Battery systems will help manage power demand during operations, including dynamic positioning, while a hydrogen dual-fuel auxiliary generator will complement three ABC Evolve main generator sets. These generators are designed to accommodate different fuel configurations, including biodiesel, hydrotreated vegetable oil (HVO) and gas-based operation, providing flexibility as alternative marine fuels develop. The vessels are also designed for extended offshore assignments, with accommodation facilities and fuel capacity intended to support deployments lasting up to 150 days. This combination of onboard capacity, specialised equipment and operational endurance is aimed at allowing Windcat to serve different segments of the offshore energy industry with the same vessel platform. “The decision to order a second MP-ASV reflects our confidence in this new vessel concept and our ambition to further strengthen our position in the offshore energy market,” said Willem van der Wel, Managing Director of Windcat. Joost van der Weiden, Sales Director at Damen, also welcomed the additional contract, highlighting the continued development of the companies’ partnership following their work on the Elevation Series. Neither the contract value nor the delivery date for the second vessel was disclosed.

Amirhosein Khorgooi/ISNA/via WANA (West Asia News Agency) via REUTERS By Weilun Soon Nov 26, 2026 (Bloomberg) –Tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has risen this month, according to data from Vortexa , even as attacks on vessels in the contested waterway have increased. The Vortexa data also show the amount of very large crude carriers and Suezmaxes crossing the strait has decreased slightly, while the number of smaller vessels has risen. Iran has launched a wave of attacks on tankers, while widening the scope of vessels it says shouldn’t be transiting the waterway to include tugboats . Meanwhile, the cost to shuttle oil through the strait and additional insurance fees have also risen to near war-time highs, a reflection of the risks shipowners are taking to make the passage. articles.summary: At least one crew member aboard a ship carrying diesel has died after the vessel capsized and partially sank off the Spanish island of Ibiza on Thursday, regional authorities said, adding there were no signs of pollution so far.

Spanish Transport Ministry/via Reuters TV/Handout via REUTERS THIS IMAGE HAS BEEN SUPPLIED BY A THIRD PARTY MADRID, Nov 26 (Reuters) – At least one crew member aboard a ship carrying diesel has died after the vessel capsized and partially sank off the Spanish island of Ibiza on Thursday, regional authorities said, adding there were no signs of pollution so far. The Malta-flagged chemical tanker Med Emre was sailing from Algeciras to Barcelona and may have been carrying up to 7,000 metric tons of diesel when it keeled over about 30 nautical miles (56 km) off Ibiza’s northwestern coast, the Balearic Islands’ interior department said. Emergency services said all 17 crew members were rescued, but one died after being taken directly to Ibiza’s Can Misses hospital. Six others were brought to Ibiza airport and taken to two hospitals with light injuries, primarily hypothermia. Of the remaining crew, five were taken to Valencia and five remained in good condition aboard a rescue vessel, they added. Pablo Garriz, the Balearic Islands’ regional head of emergencies, said the crew included Turkish and Indian nationals, but he could not yet confirm the nationality of the deceased. The tanker remained partially submerged with its keel protruding above the surface, Garriz told reporters, despite initial indications that it had sunk completely. “The positive news is that the vessel is not on the seabed but remains semi-submerged at the surface, which allows salvage and containment operations,” he said, adding there was currently no impact on Balearic waters or coastline and no evidence of a significant spill, although small sheens had been observed. Technical experts were assessing the vessel’s stability before deciding on salvage and cargo-recovery operations, he added. Spain’s maritime rescue service sent an aircraft and a vessel specialized in oil-spill response, the Clara Campoamor, to survey the area. Three helicopters took part in the rescue, along with nearby merchant vessels. Spain’s merchant marine authority activated the national maritime pollution contingency plan at level 2, the second-highest. The waters surrounding Ibiza are a habitat for sea turtles, dolphins and the Balearic shearwater, one of Europe’s most threatened seabirds. The area is also home to extensive meadows of Posidonia oceanica seagrass, which plays a vital role in supporting marine biodiversity. Spain’s worst maritime environmental disaster occurred in 2002, when the Bahamas-flagged tanker Prestige sank off the northwestern Galicia region, spilling tens of thousands of tons of heavy fuel oil and fouling hundreds of beaches in Spain and France. The Balearic regional government said it was gathering information on the accident and its possible consequences, including any risk of fuel pollution, before deciding on further measures. articles.title: Suez Canal revenues double as vessel traffic rises in November
articles.summary: Suez Canal revenues have more than doubled in November 2026 compared with the same period last year, as the waterway records a recovery in vessel traffic amid the gradual return of major shipping lines. According to figures released by the Suez Canal Authority (SCA) on 24 November, the waterway generated US$593...
articles.body: Suez Canal revenues have more than doubled in November 2026 compared with the same period last year, as the waterway records a recovery in vessel traffic amid the gradual return of major shipping lines. According to figures released by the Suez Canal Authority (SCA) on 24 November, the waterway generated US$593 million in revenue since the beginning of the month, up 101.2% from US$295 million during the corresponding period in 2025. A total of 1,194 vessels transited the canal over the reporting period, compared with 886 a year earlier, representing an increase of 34.8%. Net tonnage also rose significantly, reaching 72 million tonnes against 37 million tonnes last year. The figures were presented by SCA Chairman Ossama Rabiee during a visit to the South Red Sea Shipyard in Safaga, where the authority marked progress on several marine construction projects. The improvement comes as international shipping companies gradually restore services through the Red Sea and Suez Canal. Recent developments include the return of additional Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd services under the Gemini Cooperation , alongside renewed transits by other major container carriers. The gradual return of container carriers is also reflected in Hapag-Lloyd’s recent activity. According to the Suez Canal Authority, 30 of the German carrier’s vessels transited the waterway between August and 23 November 2026, representing a combined net tonnage of 4.8 million tonnes. Although the latest figures point to stronger activity, the SCA has not provided a breakdown of container ship transits or revenue contributions by vessel type for the reporting period. SCA expands shipbuilding ambitions Alongside the traffic figures, Rabiee outlined plans to double the production capacity of SCA-affiliated shipyards and companies, targeting the launch of two marine units per month. The authority is also aiming to build 50 tugboats for export as part of its efforts to expand Egypt’s domestic shipbuilding industry. During the visit to Safaga, trials began for two AZM-class tugboats with a bollard pull of 90 tonnes each. These are the seventh and eighth vessels in an initial programme of ten tugboats. The shipyard also launched two REZK-class deep-sea fishing vessels, REZK 4 and REZK 5. Each measures 50 metres in length and is being built under the supervision of classification society RINA. According to the SCA, two additional AZM-class tugboats are expected to be delivered to Italy’s NERI Group, while a further contract covering four tugboats is under consideration. The authority views the expansion of domestic shipbuilding as an opportunity to strengthen Egypt’s marine engineering capabilities and increase exports of specialised vessels.

Published this week, the clause covers conventional and gas tankers, including cargo transfers involving onshore and offshore installations. Under the wording, charterers ordering such operations will be responsible for the necessary equipment, regulatory permissions and associated expenses. Shipowners can also recover additional insurance premiums and other documented expenses arising from the operations, subject to prior approval from charterers. The clause allows owners to appoint a specialist mooring master or superintendent at the charterer’s expense when deemed necessary by the ship’s master. The provision was originally developed for BIMCO’s CO2TIME 2026 charterparty, adopted in April for the emerging liquefied carbon dioxide shipping market. BIMCO subsequently opted to make the clause available separately for wider use across the tanker sector. The organisation stressed that the provision does not address sanctions compliance and should be used alongside appropriate sanctions clauses where necessary. articles.title: Polish offshore wind rules draw Danish shipowner backlash
articles.summary: Danish shipowners have raised concerns at EU level over new Polish vessel certification requirements, warning that additional inspections are making it harder for foreign operators to compete for offshore wind and marine construction contracts in the Baltic Sea.
